data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The night-time UHI is fundamentally an atmospheric boundary layer depth effect, where calm clear nights form a much shallower stable boundary layer over rural areas, concentrating urban heat in a thinner layer; the UHI gap scales inversely with wind speed and boundary layer depth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If strong nocturnal winds mechanically mix the lower atmosphere uniformly to a great height in both city and country, the shallow rural boundary layer is destroyed and the UHI vanishes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If turbulent mixing in the city fails to erode a local stable layer, the heat is not trapped in the surface layer, reducing the near-surface anomaly.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Rural nocturnal cooling generates a shallow, stably stratified boundary layer near the ground, trapping cooled air. Urban surfaces emit stored sensible heat and anthropogenic heat, maintaining a warmer, well-mixed urban boundary layer. Because the rural boundary layer is so shallow, even a moderate urban heat flux produces a large near-surface temperature differential. The cross-city variance depends on local meteorology: cities with lower nocturnal wind speeds and greater atmospheric stability experience a shallower rural boundary layer, resulting in a stronger, more pronounced UHI.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
